reader_situation: A US or Canadian household opens an electric bill roughly twice the usual amount and is sure nothing at home changed. They want to know whether it is the price, the billing, the weather, or a failing appliance, and what they can make the utility or retailer do about it.
direct_answer: Split the bill into three numbers: days billed, kWh per day, and cents per kWh. A doubled total with similar kWh per day is a price or billing problem (an expired fixed-rate plan, a tier, a budget-billing settle-up, or an estimated-read catch-up). A jump in kWh per day is weather or equipment, most often heat-pump backup strips or a new resistance heater.
consensus: Compare kWh used, not just the dollar total, against the same month last year
Rate increases and expired promotional or fixed-rate plans can raise the bill with no change in use
Extreme heat or cold makes heating and cooling run more
Estimated bills can be followed by a large catch-up bill
A failing appliance such as a water heater, fridge, or pump can run nonstop
gaps: Billing days change the total on their own: Manitoba Hydro lists the number of days in a billing period and actual-versus-estimated reads among the reasons a bill is high; on SCE's tiered plan the Tier 1 allocation is the daily baseline multiplied by the number of days in the billing period.
Three ratios multiply: (days this bill / days last bill) x (kWh per day ratio) x (cents per kWh ratio) = bill ratio. Modest changes in each can compound to a doubling.

Texas specifics: since HB 16 (2021) retailers may not sell wholesale indexed products to residential customers; a fixed-rate customer must receive at least three written expiration notices in the last third of the contract, the last at least 30 days before expiration for contracts over four months; if the customer does nothing they move to a month-to-month default product whose price can vary each billing cycle and which can be cancelled without a fee; if the retailer failed to send proper notice it must keep billing at the fixed-rate pricing.

Tiered rates: SCE starts every billing period at Tier 1 (30 cents per kWh, current rates as of 10/1/26) and charges Tier 2 (39 cents) above the baseline; the daily baseline is different in summer months (June-September), so the same kWh can cost more in a different season.

Estimated billing has limits in some states: Pennsylvania's rule says bills should be based on actual reads, allows estimates every other month for monthly billing if the customer can report a reading, requires an actual or customer reading at least every 6 months (or four billing periods) when access is the problem and an actual read at least once every 12 months; a rebill that exceeds the normal estimate by at least 50% or $50 triggers the make-up bill rule (52 Pa. Code 56.14).
Budget or equal-payment plans have a settle-up month: Manitoba Hydro's August bill combines that month's charges with the credit or amount owed for the plan year.

Weather can be checked with degree days: EIA defines heating and cooling degree days from a 65 F base, and some utilities print them on bills; compare degree days for this bill to the same bill last year before blaming equipment.

Heat-pump backup heat: Emergency mode forces the system to rely 100% on heat strips (GVEC); raising the thermostat more than two degrees at once can bring on strips; NYSERDA says modern heat pumps are three times more efficient than electric resistance heat, so hours on strips cost roughly three times as much for the same heat.

Meter tests are available on request: Florida's electric rule gives a free test if the meter was not tested in the prior 12 months, otherwise a deposit up to $100 that is refunded if the meter is fast beyond the allowed limit.

evidence.claim: Texas bans wholesale indexed electricity products for residential customers
evidence.detail: Sec. 39.110(b): an aggregator, broker, or retail electric provider 'may not offer a wholesale indexed product to a residential or small commercial customer.'
evidence.source_title: H.B. No. 16 (87th Texas Legislature), enrolled text

evidence.detail: Sec. 39.112(b): at least three written notices of the expiration date, during the last third of the contract period; final notice at least 30 days before expiration for contracts longer than four months, at least 15 days for contracts under four months.
evidence.source_title: H.B. No. 16 (87th Texas Legislature), enrolled text

evidence.claim: Texas default renewal product after a fixed rate expires
evidence.detail: Sec. 39.112(h): if the customer picks no new product, the provider shall automatically serve the customer through a default renewal product, a month-to-month product in which the price may vary between billing cycles; the customer can cancel it at any time without a fee. Sec. 39.112(j): if proper expiration notice was not given, the provider must continue to serve the customer under the pricing terms of the fixed rate product until proper notice is given or the customer selects another product.
evidence.source_title: H.B. No. 16 (87th Texas Legislature), enrolled text

evidence.claim: Pennsylvania limits on estimated electric bills
evidence.detail: 52 Pa. Code 56.12: bills based on actual meter readings by utility personnel; for monthly billing the utility may estimate every other billing month if it gives the customer a chance to report a reading; when access is the problem, an actual or customer-supplied reading at least every 6 months or every four billing periods, and an actual reading at least once every 12 months; for remote-read meters an actual reading at least once every 5 years; a rebill that exceeds the normal estimate by at least 50% or $50 must comply with 56.14.
evidence.source_title: 52 Pa. Code 56.12 - Meter reading; estimated billing; customer readings (LII)

evidence.detail: 52 Pa. Code 56.12(2): resulting bills must be based on the information the customer provides unless it is apparent that it is erroneous.
evidence.source_title: 52 Pa. Code 56.12 - Meter reading; estimated billing; customer readings (LII)

evidence.claim: Florida free meter test on request (electric)
evidence.detail: Fla. Admin. Code R. 25-6.059 (Electric Service by Electric Public Utilities): the utility shall, without charge, test the meter's accuracy if it has not been tested within twelve months; more frequent requests may carry a deposit of up to $100, refunded if the meter is found fast beyond the allowed limits.
evidence.source_title: Fla. Admin. Code Ann. R. 25-6.059 - Meter Test by Request (LII)

evidence.detail: SCE Tiered Rate Plan, current rates as of 10/1/26: each billing period begins at Tier 1, 30 cents per kWh for 0-384 kWh; Tier 2, 39 cents per kWh above 100% of baseline. The allocation is the daily baseline for your region multiplied by the number of days in the billing period; the daily baseline is different in summer months (June-September).
evidence.source_title: Tiered Rate Plan for Energy | SCE

evidence.claim: Why a bill may be high (utility list)
evidence.detail: Manitoba Hydro: the August bill ends the Equal Payment Plan year and combines energy charges with a credit or amount owed; heating and cooling alone can be more than 60% of an energy bill; actual versus estimated reading and the number of days in a billing period affect charges.
evidence.source_title: Why your bill might be high | Manitoba Hydro

evidence.claim: Degree days measure weather-driven heating and cooling need
evidence.detail: EIA: base temperature 65 F; mean temperature below 65 F gives heating degree days, above gives cooling degree days. Example: high 33 F and low 25 F give a mean of 29 F, or 36 HDD. Some utilities include degree days on customer bills.
evidence.source_title: Degree days - U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA)

evidence.claim: Heat strips and emergency heat raise bills
evidence.detail: GVEC (electric cooperative): every heat pump system includes a heat strip; emergency mode forces the system to rely 100% on the heat strips; heat strips need a lot more energy to run than a heat pump; raising the thermostat more than two degrees at once can trigger strip heating.
evidence.source_title: Heat Pumps, Heat Strips and Emergency Heating | GVEC

evidence.claim: Heat pump vs. electric resistance efficiency
evidence.detail: NYSERDA: 'Modern heat pumps are three times more efficient than conventional oil, propane, or electric resistance heating.'
evidence.source_title: Heat Pumps for Cold Climates - Is It Expensive? | NYSERDA Clean Heat

real_questions: My kWh is about the same as last year, so why is the bill twice as much?
My fixed-rate plan ended and the new rate is huge; can I get out of it?
The bill says 'estimated'; do I have to pay the catch-up all at once?
Is my smart meter wrong, and can I get it tested?
Why did my heat pump bill double in a cold month?

original_asset.spec: Three-ratio breakdown: bill ratio = days ratio x kWh-per-day ratio x cents-per-kWh ratio, using a hypothetical 30-day, 900 kWh bill at the registry's 17 cents versus a 33-day bill; show how each ratio points to a cause. Followed by a decision table mapping which ratio moved to the likely cause and the document or rule to check (HB 16 notices, PA 56.12 estimates, SCE tier/days, Manitoba Hydro settle-up, EIA degree days, GVEC strips, FL meter test).

cautions: Rules quoted are state-specific (Texas, Pennsylvania, Florida); tell readers to check their own state commission or provincial regulator.
SCE tier prices are dated (as of 10/1/26) and change; present them as one utility's example.
Do not tell readers to open the meter base or electrical panel; meter problems go to the utility.
Space heaters: use the registry energy formula and rate; do not invent safety statistics.
